hints: Think of the two essential building blocks of any complex, the electron poor centre and the electron rich species that surround it.
walkthrough:
Picture what makes a complex special**
Imagine a central cobalt ion sitting in the middle with six small molecules like water arranged around it, each one attached directly to it. That whole assembly carries a charge, so we call it an ion, and the centre plus its attachments is the complex.

Name the partners correctly**
The centre must be a metal atom or ion because it has empty orbitals to accept electron pairs. The species attached to it are called ligands, and each one donates a lone pair to form a dative covalent bond to the metal.
Final answer: A complex ion is a (central) metal atom or ion surrounded by / bonded to one or more ligands.

hints: Recall the characteristic test for aqueous transition metal ions with NaOH, does a solid appear and what colour is typical for cobalt(II).
Think about what the hydroxide ion does to the hexaaqua ion, does it replace the whole water or remove H+ from coordinated water.
For excess concentrated ammonia, decide whether ammonia acts as a base to give a precipitate or as a competing ligand that stays in solution.
Count ligands to balance each ionic equation, six monodentate ligands around octahedral Co(II) must be conserved.
Compare the ligands before and after in the ammonia reaction to decide if the coordination sphere has been swapped.
Use the terms precipitation, acid-base and ligand substitution carefully to distinguish forming a hydroxide solid from swapping one neutral ligand for another.
walkthrough:
Reaction with NaOH, what you see**
When $\text{OH}^{-}$ meets pink $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, a blue solid appears. That solid is cobalt(II) hydroxide, $\text{Co(OH)}_2$. A solid forming from solution is the classic sign of precipitation.

Write the ionic equation for the hydroxide reaction**
Two $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions are needed to neutralise the 2+ charge and to replace water. In simplest form:
$$[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
This can also be written as formation of $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_4(\text{OH})_2]$. It is an acid-base or precipitation reaction, not a full ligand swap by $\text{NH}_3$, because $\text{OH}^{-}$ removes protons from coordinated water.

Reaction with excess ammonia, what you see**
With a little ammonia you would first get a blue precipitate, but in excess the precipitate redissolves to give a clear blue solution. That tells you the product is soluble, the hexaammine complex $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+}$.

Write the ionic equation for the ammonia reaction**
All six waters are directly swapped for six ammonias, with coordination number staying at six:
$$[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Because one ligand replaces another in the coordination sphere, the type is ligand exchange, also called substitution, displacement or replacement.

Final answer: With aqueous NaOH: blue precipitate / solid of cobalt-containing species; $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$; precipitation / acid-base reaction.
With excess aqueous $\text{NH}_3$: blue solution of cobalt-containing species; $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$; ligand exchange / substitution / displacement.

hints: Identify what silver ions do to free chloride ions in solution and how that changes $[\text{Cl}^{-}]$.
Apply Le Chatelier to the equilibrium $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ when a reactant concentration is lowered.
walkthrough:
Spot the side reaction that removes chloride**
Silver ions love chloride ions. As soon as you add $\text{AgNO}_3$, you get:
$$\text{Ag}^{+} + \text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s)}$$
That is the white precipitate you see. Importantly, it pulls free $\text{Cl}^{-}$ out of the cobalt equilibrium mixture.

Use Le Chatelier to predict the shift**
Look at the equilibrium:
$$[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightleftharpoons [\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Lowering $[\text{Cl}^{-}]$ is like removing a left hand side reactant. The system opposes the change by shifting left to make more $\text{Cl}^{-}$, converting blue tetrahedral $[\text{CoCl}_4]^{2-}$ back into pink octahedral $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$. So you observe blue to pink plus white $\text{AgCl}$.

Final answer: Blue solution turns pink and a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ forms. $\text{Ag}^{+}$ removes $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so $[\text{Cl}^{-}]$ decreases and the equilibrium shifts to the left, reforming pink $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$.

hints: Picture octahedral $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_3\text{Cl}_3]$ and ask how three identical ligands can be arranged, all clustered together or wrapped around the centre.
Recall the name given when the same ligands occupy adjacent positions differently in octahedral complexes, the same family as cis-trans in square planar complexes.
walkthrough:
Draw the fac isomer**
Put Co in the centre of an octahedron. In the facial isomer, the three $\text{NH}_3$ ligands sit on three corners that share one face, so every $\text{NH}_3$ is cis (90 degrees) to the other two. The three $\text{Cl}$ ligands then occupy the opposite face. It looks like two tripods back to back.

Draw the mer isomer**
In the meridional isomer, the three $\text{NH}_3$ ligands wrap around the middle like a meridian on a globe. Two of the $\text{NH}_3$ ligands are now trans (180 degrees, opposite each other) with the third cis to both. The three $\text{Cl}$ ligands do the same in the perpendicular arrangement.

Name the type**
Both have the same formula and bonds, only the spatial arrangement differs, with cis versus trans relationships. This is geometric isomerism, also accepted as cis-trans isomerism. It is not optical because these $\text{MA}_3\text{B}_3$ isomers are superimposable on their mirror images.

Final answer: fac isomer: three $\text{NH}_3$ occupy one triangular face of the octahedron (all mutually cis) and three $\text{Cl}$ occupy the opposite face. mer isomer: three $\text{NH}_3$ (and three $\text{Cl}$) lie in a meridian plane around Co, with two $\text{NH}_3$ trans to each other. Type: geometric (cis-trans) isomerism.

hints: Look at the structure of X and count the nitrogen atoms, then ask what feature on nitrogen allows it to bond to a metal.
walkthrough:
Count the donor atoms**
Look along the chain $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. There are four nitrogens, two terminal $\text{NH}_2$ groups and two central $\text{NH}$ groups. Nitrogen in an amine has three covalent bonds and one lone pair. So each N can donate its lone pair to Co to make a dative bond, giving four bonds in total, which is why X is tetradentate.
Final answer: Each of the four nitrogen atoms in X has a lone pair of electrons available to donate to the metal ion, so one molecule can form four dative bonds.

hints: Think of X replacing water molecules from $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ in a 1:1 ratio and decide how many waters must leave to accommodate four N donors.
walkthrough:
Build the substitution equation**
One tetradentate X wraps around Co(II) and ejects the six monodentate waters in a 1:1 reaction. Charge stays 2+ because X is neutral:
$$[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4 \rightarrow [\text{Co(C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4)]^{2+} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
If you show two waters remaining coordinated, $[\text{Co(C}_6\text{H}_{18}\text{N}_4)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as product is also chemically consistent with a six coordinate Co.
